claim: The V. vulnificus add riboswitch is a ~120 nucleotide element that resides in the 5´ untranslated region (UTR) of the add adenosine deaminase mRNA of human pathogenic bacterium Vibrio vulnificus.
source: A particularly well-studied – but still incompletely understood – example of an allosteric RNA is the add riboswitch, a ~120 nucleotide element that resides in the 5´ untranslated region (UTR) of the add adenosine deaminase mRNA of human pathogenic bacterium Vibrio vulnificus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on the add riboswitch system (Lemay et al., 2011; Mandal and Breaker, 2004; Batey, 2012; Cordero and Das, 2015; Stoddard et al., 2013; Rieder et al., 2007; Neupane et al., 2011; Lemay et al., 2006; Greenleaf et al., 2008; Wickiser et al., 2005; Lemay and Lafontaine, 2007; Stagno et al., 2017).

claim: The add riboswitch can directly bind adenine and controls translation of the mRNA in response to adenine in vivo.
source: This riboswitch can directly bind adenine and controls translation of the mRNA in response to adenine in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Lemay et al., 2011; Mandal and Breaker, 2004; Batey, 2012; Cordero and Das, 2015; Stoddard et al., 2013; Rieder et al., 2007; Neupane et al., 2011; Lemay et al., 2006; Greenleaf et al., 2008; Wickiser et al., 2005; Lemay and Lafontaine, 2007; Stagno et al., 2017).

claim: Almost all work on the add riboswitch to date have assumed some variation of a Monod-Wyman-Changeux model (MWC, also called 'conformational selection' or 'population shift' models).
source: Almost all work on the add riboswitch to date have assumed some variation of a Monod-Wyman-Changeux model (MWC, also called 'conformational selection' or 'population shift' models) (Monod et al., 1965; Batey, 2012; Gunasekaran et al., 2004; Changeux and Edelstein, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on MWC models and the add riboswitch (Monod et al., 1965; Batey, 2012; Gunasekaran et al., 2004; Changeux and Edelstein, 2005).

claim: In the absence of adenine, the add riboswitch RNA dominantly forms a stable apo secondary structure whose aptamer region is in a fold incompatible with adenine binding and whose gene expression platform, a ribosome binding site and AUG start codon, is sequestered into helices.
source: In the absence of adenine, the RNA dominantly forms a stable apo secondary structure whose aptamer region is in a fold incompatible with adenine binding and whose gene expression platform, a ribosome binding site and AUG start codon, is sequestered into helices (blue, Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A and is based on prior literature and knowledge of the add riboswitch mechanism.

claim: High adenine concentrations stabilize the ligand-binding secondary structure in the aptamer region and rearrange the secondary structure around the gene expression platform so that it is freed to recruit the ribosome and translation machinery.
source: High adenine concentrations stabilize the ligand-binding secondary structure in the aptamer region and rearrange the secondary structure around the gene expression platform so that it is freed to recruit the ribosome and translation machinery (gold, Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A and is based on prior literature and knowledge of the add riboswitch mechanism.

claim: The signature prediction of the MWC model is that the holo RNA secondary structure should also exist in the absence of adenine, albeit as a high energy conformation within the apo ensemble.
source: The signature prediction of the MWC model is that the holo RNA secondary structure should also exist in the absence of adenine, albeit as a high energy conformation within the apo ensemble (Figure 1A, middle panel; gold).
evidence: This claim is based on the theoretical prediction of the MWC model as applied to the add riboswitch, referencing Figure 1A.

claim: In the MWC model, when the RNA occasionally fluctuates to form an aptamer secondary structure compatible with ligand binding, the gene expression platform is predicted to concomitantly open, even without the adenine ligand.
source: In terms of the riboswitch functional domains, when the RNA occasionally fluctuates to form an aptamer secondary structure compatible with ligand binding, the gene expression platform is predicted to concomitantly open, even without the adenine ligand.
evidence: This claim is based on the theoretical prediction of the MWC model as applied to the add riboswitch.

claim: A recent study proposed a non-MWC model for the add riboswitch based on multidimensional NMR spectroscopy, NMR relaxation studies, designed model systems, and supporting measurements from stopped-flow kinetics and calorimetry.
source: Recently, a tour de force study highlighted an alternative to the MWC mechanism for the add riboswitch (Figure 1B). Multidimensional NMR spectroscopy, NMR relaxation studies, designed model systems, and supporting measurements from stopped-flow kinetics and calorimetry revealed detailed single-nucleotide-resolution base pairing information and intriguing temperature dependences for the complex structural ensemble of the add riboswitch (Reining et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the NMR study (Reining et al., 2013) and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The non-MWC model proposed that, in the absence of adenine, riboswitches that sample the correct aptameric secondary structure do not also concomitantly open their ribosome binding sites and increase gene expression.
source: Although similar in some respects to previously proposed MWC models, the new model contradicted a standard MWC assumption (Gunasekaran et al., 2004; Changeux and Edelstein, 2005; Eaton et al., 1999): it proposed that, in the absence of adenine, riboswitches that sample the correct aptameric secondary structure do not also concomitantly open their ribosome binding sites and increase gene expression, as predicted by MWC conformational selection (Figure 1B, middle panel; mixed blue and gold, red rectangle outline).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the NMR study (Reining et al., 2013) and references to prior MWC literature (Gunasekaran et al., 2004; Changeux and Edelstein, 2005; Eaton et al., 1999), as well as Figure 1B.

claim: The same group that first proposed a non-MWC model for the add RNA has recently revived the MWC framework to interpret newer single molecule measurements on the same system.
source: As an illustration of current uncertainties in the system, the same group that first proposed an non-MWC model for the add RNA has recently revived the MWC framework to interpret newer single molecule measurements on the same system (Warhaut et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the single molecule study (Warhaut et al., 2017).

claim: Lock-mutate-map-rescue (LM2R) is a four-dimensional expansion of chemical mapping that integrates multiple layers of mutation with nucleotide-resolution chemical mapping.
source: Here, we present a four-dimensional expansion of chemical mapping called lock-mutate-map-rescue (LM2R), which integrates multiple layers of mutation with nucleotide-resolution chemical mapping.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and is the main methodological contribution of the manuscript.

claim: LM2R measurements give strong support to the pre-existing correlations predicted by MWC models for the add riboswitch.
source: These LM2R measurements give strong support to the pre-existing correlations predicted by MWC models, disfavor alternative models, and suggest additional structural heterogeneities that may be general across ligand-free riboswitches.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental LM2R data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: LM2R measurements disfavor non-MWC alternative models for the add riboswitch.
source: These LM2R measurements give strong support to the pre-existing correlations predicted by MWC models, disfavor alternative models, and suggest additional structural heterogeneities that may be general across ligand-free riboswitches.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental LM2R data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: LM2R measurements suggest additional structural heterogeneities that may be general across ligand-free riboswitches.
source: These LM2R measurements give strong support to the pre-existing correlations predicted by MWC models, disfavor alternative models, and suggest additional structural heterogeneities that may be general across ligand-free riboswitches.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental LM2R data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 7G-I showing weak or no correlation between helices expected to co-occur in apoB.

claim: Compensatory mutation experiments integrated with chemical mapping readouts (mutate-map-rescue, M2R) enable incisive confirmation or falsification of candidate base pairs.
source: Mutate-map-rescue (M2R) experiments (Figure 2) enable incisive confirmation or falsification of candidate base pairs.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work on M2R (Tian et al., 2014; Tian and Das, 2016) and is illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Strong evidence for a candidate base pair comes from observations that mutation of either side of a base pair disrupts the SHAPE profile of the RNA and that the compensatory double mutation restores the SHAPE measurements to the wild type profile.
source: Strong evidence for a candidate base pair comes from observations that mutation of either side of a base pair (mutant A or mutant B) disrupts the SHAPE profile of the RNA; and that the compensatory double mutation (mutant AB) restores the SHAPE measurements to the wild type (WT) profile.
evidence: This claim is based on the M2R methodology described in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Partial rescue in M2R experiments is a hallmark of base pairs that are present at low frequency in an RNA's structural ensemble.
source: In our studies on the 16S rRNA four-way junction, the strongly populated helix shift-P4a was associated with mutate-map-rescue data that showed unambiguous rescue while the less populated helix P4a was associated with 'partial' rescue. In the latter case, disruptions in SHAPE reactivity induced by single mutations were alleviated by their concomitant compensatory mutation, but new features distinct from the wild type SHAPE profile also appeared (yellow arrow, bottom panel of Figure 2A). We speculated that such 'partial rescue' might generally be a hallmark of base pairs that are present at low frequency in an RNA's structural ensemble.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work on the 16S rRNA (Tian et al., 2014) and is illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: In silico tests confirmed that observation of strong rescue over all the base pairs of a helix implies high helix frequency.
source: These in silico tests confirmed that observation of strong rescue over all the base pairs of a helix implies high helix frequency (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Averaging rescue factors over tests on three or more base pairs gave values that showed a striking correlation with helix frequencies in simulations.
source: As expected, individual base pair tests were noisy, but averaging rescue factors over tests on three or more base pairs gave values that showed a striking correlation with helix frequencies (compare gray and black points, Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Absence of rescue (rescue factor close to zero) gave upper bounds on the helix frequency in simulations.
source: Furthermore, absence of rescue (rescue factor close to zero; Figure 2D, bottom) gave upper bounds on the helix frequency (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation data presented in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the absence of adenine, the add riboswitch shows a diverse set of helices including aptamer helices P1 (53%) and P2 (31%).
source: In the absence of adenine, all prior models of the add riboswitch predicted that the RNA would show a diverse set of helices. Indeed, aptamer helices P1 (53%) and P2 (31%) were detectable, as they gave partial rescue in mutate-map-rescue experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by the M2R experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 3A and Figure 4.

claim: Helices P3 and P5 were detected by compensatory rescue experiments in the absence of adenine, with median helix frequencies of 73% and 75%, respectively.
source: Helices P3 and P5 were expected to be present, and both were detected by compensatory rescue experiments, with median helix frequencies of 73% and 75%, respectively (brown curves, Figure 4; Figure 3—figure supplement 1 gives SHAPE profiles).
evidence: This claim is supported by the M2R experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Compensatory rescue experiments recovered evidence for helices P4A (48%), P4B (55%), P4C (68%), P1B (44%), and P2B (17%) in the absence of adenine.
source: In addition, compensatory rescue experiments recovered evidence for helices P4A (48%), P4B (55%), P4C (68%), P1B (44%), and, at a lower level, P2B (17%), all proposed as part of apoB (Figure 1; left-hand structure in top panel, Figure 3; Figure 3B shows SHAPE profiles and associated partial rescue for each base pair of P4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the M2R experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 3B and Figure 4.

claim: In the presence of 5 mM adenine, SHAPE measurements for single and compensatory mutations targeting helices P1, P2, P3, and P5 gave helix frequencies of 79%, 64%, 56% and 29%, respectively.
source: Indeed, in the presence of 5 mM adenine, SHAPE measurements for single and compensatory mutations targeting these helices and rescue factor analysis gave helix frequencies of 79%, 64%, 56% and 29%, respectively (Figure 3C; and gold and brown curves in Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the M2R experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 3C and Figure 4C and D.

claim: Measuring rescue factors for helices P1B, P2B, P4A, P4B, and P4C in the presence of adenine gave no evidence for their presence.
source: Measuring rescue factors for other helices, including P1B, P2B, P4A, P4B, and P4C predicted for the adenine-free state and other helices proposed to occur at low frequencies from M2-guided modeling (P6, P8 through P17) (Cordero and Das, 2015), gave no evidence for their presence when adenine was bound (example SHAPE profile quartets for P4B in Figure 3D; all quartets in Figure 3—figure supplement 1; and blue and pink curves, Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the M2R experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 3D and Figure 4C and D.

claim: Locking P4B strongly reduces P1 helix frequency in the absence of adenine.
source: The inferred P4B helix frequency drops from 53%% to 5%; the shift in posterior probability distribution to lower helix frequency values is clear (faded gold to gold curves; Figure 6B). Stated simply, locking P4B strongly reduces P1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the LM2R experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 6A and B.

claim: The posterior support for non-MWC models (g(P1,P4B)>1) from the lock-P4B experiment is 3.1 × 10–3.
source: This posterior support is small, with a value of 3.1 × 10–3, disfavoring the non-MWC model and supporting the MWC model.
evidence: This claim is supported by the LM2R experimental data and Bayesian analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Upon locking P1, the P4B helix frequency drops from 55% to 4%.
source: Again, in contrast to the observation of partial rescue of P4B in the wild type RNA (Figure 3B), the data in the lock-P1 context show no rescue for P4B. Upon locking P1, the P4B helix frequency drops, from 55% to 4%, and there is a striking shift in the posterior probability distribution to lower helix frequencies (faded blue to blue curves; Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the LM2R experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 6D.

claim: When the data for the lock-P4B and lock-P1 experiments are combined, the posterior support for the non-MWC model becomes 4 × 10–5.
source: If the data for the two experiments are combined, the posterior support for the non-MWC model becomes quite small, 4 × 10–5.
evidence: This claim is supported by the LM2R experimental data and Bayesian analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The posterior support for the non-MWC model from the P2-P4B correlation experiments is 1.5 × 10–3.
source: These results again strongly disfavor the non-MWC model (posterior support: 4.1 × 10–3 and 1.5 × 10–3, respectively) and supporting the MWC model.
evidence: This claim is supported by the LM2R experimental data and Bayesian analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The posterior support for the non-MWC model from the P2-P4A correlation experiments is 4.1 × 10–3.
source: These results again strongly disfavor the non-MWC model (posterior support: 4.1 × 10–3 and 1.5 × 10–3, respectively) and supporting the MWC model.
evidence: This claim is supported by the LM2R experimental data and Bayesian analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: LM2R experiments gave no evidence of correlation for pairs of helices expected to co-occur in the riboswitch when the aptamer secondary structure is not formed (apoB).
source: On the other hand, we saw no evidence of correlation for pairs of helices expected to co-occur in the riboswitch when the aptamer secondary structure is not formed (apoB, Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the LM2R experimental data and Bayesian analysis presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 7G-I.

claim: The data are most consistent with a model in which helices P4A, P1B, P4B each appear with significant frequency in the apo ensemble, but do not necessarily co-occur, resulting in a heterogeneous structural ensemble.
source: While the uncertainties in these LM2R measurements allow correlation values of these helices to be slightly greater than 1, the data are most consistent with a model in which helices P4A, P1B, P4B each appear with significant frequency in the apo ensemble, but do not necessarily co-occur, resulting a heterogeneous structural ensemble.
evidence: This claim is supported by the LM2R experimental data and Bayesian analysis presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 7G-I.

claim: A single secondary structure such as apoB may not be an appropriate description of the structural ensemble.
source: Therefore, a single secondary structure such as apoB may not be an appropriate description of the structural ensemble.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the LM2R experimental data showing no correlation between helices expected to co-occur in apoB.

claim: Lock-P4A and lock-P1B showed reproducible differences in SHAPE reactivities at the 5´ end of the RNA (nts 13–20) that were larger than differences between lock-P1 and lock-P2.
source: Further evidence for structural heterogeneity came from the incomplete match in SHAPE profiles for mutants that lock different helices of the putative apoB state. For example, lock-P4A and lock-P1B showed reproducible differences in SHAPE reactivities at the 5´ end of the RNA (nts 13–20) that were larger than, e.g., differences between lock-P1 and lock-P2 (Figure 5), and we did not discover any alternative locking mutations that brought them into agreement.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental SHAPE data presented in Figure 5.

claim: The proposed model favors a Monod-Wyman-Changeux (population shift, conformational selection) model of allostery for the add riboswitch.
source: The proposed model favors a Monod-Wyman-Changeux (population shift, conformational selection) model of allostery.
evidence: This claim is supported by the LM2R experimental data presented throughout the manuscript and is summarized in Figure 8.

claim: The measurements show that sampling of the aptamer secondary structure is strongly anticorrelated with formation of the P4 domain.
source: Our measurements show that sampling of the aptamer secondary structure is strongly anticorrelated with formation of the P4 domain; it is therefore valid to represent it as a separate state (apoA, middle).
evidence: This claim is supported by the LM2R experimental data presented in Figures 6 and 7 and is summarized in Figure 8.

claim: The apoA state is structurally similar to the ligand-bound holo, including not just the aptamer region but also the gene expression platform, as predicted by an MWC framework.
source: This apoA state is structurally similar to the ligand-bound holo, including not just the aptamer region but also the gene expression platform, as predicted by an MWC framework (right).
evidence: This claim is supported by the LM2R experimental data presented in Figures 6 and 7 and is summarized in Figure 8.

claim: The measurements and other studies are consistent with sampling of additional alternative structures in the apoB state.
source: Our measurements and other studies are consistent with sampling of additional alternative structures in the apoB state (dashed blue lines), a partially formed P5 in apoA, and additional stabilization of the aptamer through coupled tertiary contacts upon adenine binding (dashed black lines in apoA, solid yellow lines in holo).
evidence: This claim is supported by the LM2R experimental data presented in Figure 7G-I and is summarized in Figure 8.

claim: Newer single molecule FRET measurements detect transient formation of the L2/L3 tertiary contact prior to adenine binding and stabilization upon adenine binding to holo.
source: Sixth, newer single molecule FRET measurements detect transient formation of the L2/L3 tertiary contact prior to adenine binding (dashed lines in apoA of Figure 6) and stabilization upon adenine binding to holo (Warhaut et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the single molecule FRET study (Warhaut et al., 2017).

claim: The single molecule FRET data are consistent with an MWC framework in which formation of the aptameric secondary structure occurs in concert with opening of the gene expression platform, even without adenine ligand present.
source: These data are consistent with, and indeed were interpreted within, an MWC framework in which formation of the aptameric secondary structure occurs in concert with opening of the gene expression platform, even without adenine ligand present (Warhaut et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the single molecule FRET study (Warhaut et al., 2017).

claim: There is now concordance across numerous measurements for an MWC model that posits strong secondary structure similarities between an apoA state that transiently forms the aptamer secondary structure without adenine ligand and the ligand-bound holo state.
source: There is now concordance across numerous measurements for an MWC model that posits strong secondary structure similarities between an apoA state that transiently forms the aptamer secondary structure without adenine ligand and the ligand-bound holo state.
evidence: This claim is supported by the LM2R experimental data presented in the manuscript and by comparison to prior literature.

claim: Further heterogeneity is likely to be present in members of the apo ensemble that do not present the aptamer secondary structure, grouped into apoB.
source: We also propose herein that further heterogeneity is likely to be present in members of the apo ensemble that do not present the aptamer secondary structure, grouped into apoB.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the LM2R experimental data showing no correlation between helices expected to co-occur in apoB (Figure 7G-I).

claim: The presence of myriad alternative helices, each at low population, would explain their detection difficulty with bulk equilibrium techniques but their appearance in single-molecule measurements.
source: The presence of these myriad alternative helices, each at low population, would explain their detection difficulty with this and prior bulk equilibrium techniques but their appearance in single-molecule measurements (Neupane et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the LM2R experimental data and is supported by citation to single-molecule measurements (Neupane et al., 2011).

claim: Higher-order M2 analysis in single mutant backgrounds isolate and confirm numerous alternative secondary structures for the add riboswitch.
source: Supporting this picture, higher-order M2 analysis in single mutant backgrounds isolate and confirm numerous alternative secondary structures for the add riboswitch (Figure 8—figure supplement 2 and Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental M2 data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 2 and Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: There are no functional reasons for the apoB ensemble to maintain a single secondary structure – it simply has to disallow adenine binding while keeping the gene expression platform closed in P4.
source: We note that there are no functional reasons for the apoB ensemble to maintain a single secondary structure – it simply has to disallow adenine binding while keeping the gene expression platform closed in P4.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the functional requirements of the apoB state.

claim: Without selection for a pure single structure, apoB has remained structurally heterogeneous, and the exact populations of its helix pairings outside the P4 domain may shift in different solution conditions and flanking sequences while still being compatible with riboswitch function.
source: Without selection for a pure single structure, we therefore suggest that apoB has remained structurally heterogeneous, and the exact populations of its helix pairings outside the P4 domain may shift in different solution conditions and flanking sequences while still being compatible with riboswitch function.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the LM2R experimental data showing no correlation between helices expected to co-occur in apoB.

claim: 'Non-functional' states of other riboswitches and RNA gene regulatory modules may have highly heterogeneous structures, which might explain why those states have been refractory to conventional structural biology approaches developed primarily to dissect protein structure/function.
source: We further speculate that 'non-functional' states of other riboswitches and RNA gene regulatory modules may have highly heterogeneous structures and, indeed, this feature might explain why those states have been refractory to conventional structural biology approaches developed primarily to dissect protein structure/function.
evidence: This claim is speculative and is based on inference from the LM2R experimental data on the add riboswitch.

claim: Antibiotics targeting any specific apo structure of the add and other riboswitches are unlikely to succeed, as single mutations that disrupt the targeted apo structure while retaining other members of the apo ensemble with the P4 domain could evolve quickly and offer resistance.
source: This picture also implies that antibiotics targeting any specific apo structure of the add and other riboswitches are unlikely to succeed, as single mutations that disrupt the targeted apo structure while retaining other members of the apo ensemble with the P4 domain could evolve quickly and offer resistance.
evidence: This claim is speculative and is based on inference from the LM2R experimental data showing structural heterogeneity in the apo ensemble.

claim: Double-stranded DNA templates were prepared by PCR assembly of DNA oligomers with maximum length of 60 nt ordered from IDT.
source: Double-stranded DNA templates were prepared by PCR assembly of DNA oligomers with maximum length of 60 nt ordered from IDT (Integrated DNA Technologies).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: The 128-nt construct was used for all measurements in this manuscript.
source: The 128-nt construct was therefore used for all measurements in this manuscript.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods used in the study and is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Measurements were acquired in 10 mM MgCl2, 50 mM Na-HEPES, pH 8.0, in the absence or presence of ligand (5 mM adenine).
source: Measurements were acquired in 10 mM MgCl2, 50 mM Na-HEPES, pH 8.0, in the absence or presence of ligand (5 mM adenine).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental conditions used in the study.

claim: All chemical mapping datasets have been deposited at the RNA Mapping Database (http://rmdb.stanford.edu) under specified accession codes.
source: All chemical mapping datasets, including M2, M2R, LM2R and multi-probe mapping, have been deposited at the RNA Mapping Database (http://rmdb.stanford.edu) (Cordero et al., 2012a) under the following accession codes: ADD140_1M7_0001, ADD140_1M7_0002, ADD140_1M7_0003, ADD140_1M7_0004, ADD140_1M7_0005, ADD140_1M7_0006, ADD140_1M7_0007,ADD140_1M7_0008, ADD140_1M7_0009, ADD140_1M7_0010, ADD140_1M7_0011, ADD140_1M7_0012, ADD140_1M7_0013, ADD140_1M7_0014, ADD140_RSQ_0001, ADD140_RSQ_0002, ADD140_RSQ_0003, ADD140_RSQ_0004, ADD140_LCK_0001, ADD140_LCK_0002, ADD140_LCK_0003, ADD140_LCK_0004, ADD140_LCK_0005, ADD140_LCK_0006, ADD71_STD_0001, ADD128_STD_0001, ADD140_STD_0001, ADD140_DCP_0001, ADD140_DCP_0002, RNAPZ5_RSQ_0001, TRP4P6_RSQ_0001, 16SFWJ_RSQ_0001.
evidence: This claim describes the data availability for the study.

claim: All RNA families with length between 100 and 250 nt were screened from the Rfam database 11.0 FASTA file.
source: All RNA families with length between 100 and 250 nt were screened from the Rfam database (http://rfam.xfam.org/) 11.0 FASTA file (Burge et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim describes the simulation methods used in the study.

claim: The MATLAB source code for Rfam simulation and rescue factor estimates are available in a GitHub repository: https://github.com/DasLab/m2r_simulations/.
source: The MATLAB source code for Rfam simulation and rescue factor estimates are available in a GitHub repository: https://github.com/DasLab/m2r_simulations/.
evidence: This claim describes the code availability for the study.
